chapter.title: Talking to Python Objects
chapter.para: A Python object in Rexx is used with Rexx messages: an attribute is a message, a call is a message with arguments, and items, operators and DO OVER are Python's. This chapter shows the forms.

section.title: Python Names from Rexx
section.para: You want to reach Python's names, which are case-sensitive, from Rexx, whose symbols are uppercase.

How it works. Rexx sends COUNTER and MOST_COMMON; the bridge looks the name up without regard to case, so it finds Counter and most_common. When several names match, the one in lowercase wins, if it is the only one. o~getattr("name") takes the exact name, and returns the attribute itself, never called: here the method, which ~new(1) then calls. new on a Python object calls it, as Python's o(...) does: a class makes an instance, a function or a method runs.

A function used without arguments is called (math~pi is a value, but uuid~uuid4 calls the function); a class or a module is returned, so that its attributes can be reached: np~linalg~det(m), io~StringIO~new.
See also Reference, Messages to Python Objects.

section.title: Keyword Arguments
section.para: You want to pass key=, reverse=True, base=16: Python's keyword arguments.

How it works. Rexx has no keyword arguments, so they go in a marker, the last argument of the call: .py~kw(name, value, ...), or the routine py.kw(...), or .py~kw(aDirectory) to make them from a Directory. The names go as written, in their case. Only the marker is taken as keywords: a Directory at the end of the arguments, without kw, is passed as itself.

.true is the Rexx string 1, so it goes to reverse as the int 1, which Python takes as true; a parameter that a Python function annotates as bool gets True instead (). A Rexx Array, such as words here, goes to Python as a list.

section.title: Items and Iteration
section.para: You want a dict's values, a list's items, and to loop over them.

How it works. o[k] and o[k] = v are Python's indexing, and do x over o is Python's for x in o: over a dict, its keys. A Rexx Array goes to Python as a list, nested Arrays as nested lists (and a multi-dimensional Array as lists nested by dimension). A list's positions count from 0, as in Python: it is Python's object, and Python's indexing (negative positions, slices, numpy's tuples) needs it.
The average is Rexx's arithmetic, on the Rexx strings that sum and len return; so it has Rexx's nine digits.
See also Reference, Items and Slices.

section.title: Slices
section.para: How it works. Rexx has no : in brackets, so a slice is made with Python's builtin slice: .py~slice(2, 8, 2) is 2:8:2, and .nil leaves a part out. Assigning to a slice replaces it. Several indexes in brackets are a tuple, as numpy wants: m[.py~slice(0, 2), 1] is m[0:2, 1].
The text is made a Python str first: a Rexx string's own [] is Rexx's, which does not slice.
See also Reference, Items and Slices.

section.title: A Python List as a Rexx Array
section.para: You want to use a Python list the Rexx way, counting from 1.

How it works. o~makeArrayProxy returns a PyArrayProxy: an object with the methods of a Rexx Array ([], at, put, items, append, remove, DO OVER...), counting from 1, that reads and writes the Python list itself: nothing is copied, and the list changes. It works on any Python sequence: a list, a tuple (read only), a one-dimensional numpy array.
